keyboard.topText:
The books in the CLEVER KEYS! series work from cover to cover towards building a strong foundation of knowledge that will support children as their musical interests grow.

They have been written with the intention of allowing easy, intuitive navigation and progression as a student works through the content – with or without a teacher. The books can be used in a classroom setting (for both individual and group lessons), at home as a parent/child activity or as a fun, challenging activity book for more advanced children to work through independently. The material is delivered in a clear, accessible way and the elements of theory and technique are sandwiched throughout by fun activities sure to engage and entertain the children as they learn.

Each book contains a mixture of written exercises, aural and sight-reading challenges, songs and theory worksheets – in addition to their primary musical benefits, the various activities in CLEVER KEYS! books also promote the development of memory skills, coordination, and good fine motor function.
keyboard.introText:
CLEVER KEYS! Introduction serves as a very-first-steps volume that can be used for younger children who wish to learn either Piano or Electronic Keyboard. It introduces students to simple music notation & reading guided by colour coding, focusing primarily on right-hand playing for both Piano and Electronic Keyboard, and a short section on left-hand playing is included toward the end of the books. Using brand new compositions, as well as family favourites like Twinkle Twinkle Little Star and Hot Cross Buns, children are introduced to the basic properties of melody, pitch and rhythm.

CLEVER KEYS! Introduction contains progressive learning material, a Theory Book summarising all key concepts learned throughout the book, Star Charts to track each student’s progress and a dedicated Notebook at the back for teacher/student notes.

Upon completion of this book, children will be equipped to progress along either the Electronic Keyboard or the Piano pathway. More advanced students are advised to skip this volume and start right away with the Beginner for their desired instrument!
keyboard.beginText:
CLEVER KEYS! Beginner Keyboard serves as a thorough introduction volume to music theory and Electronic Keyboard playing. It introduces the concepts of rhythm & pitch, melody & accompaniment, scales, fingered chord technique and more... Younger students are advised to start with CLEVER KEYS! Introduction for a slower paced introduction to some of these topics!

CLEVER KEYS! Beginner Keyboard contains progressive learning material, a Song Book containing both new, original compositions and traditional family favourites, a Theory Book summarising all key concepts learned throughout the book, a Chord Bank for easy revision of chords and a dedicated Notebook at the back for teacher/student notes.

Upon completion of this book, children will be equipped to progress on to CLEVER KEYS! Intermediate Keyboard and CLEVER KEYS! Advanced Keyboard - Coming Soon!

general.diffTitle: Electronic Keyboard or Piano - What's the Difference?
general.diffText:
There are a number of differences between piano and electronic keyboard and in turn, the techniques that are employed to teach each instrument. Essentially, the main differences are that a piano is traditionally an acoustic instrument (i.e. the body of the instrument itself generates its sound) with weighted keys, where an electronic keyboard requires a power source to generate its sound, they often have a vast array of instrument tones available (i.e. you can set your keyboard to sound like horns, flutes, voices, drums and more) and has lighter weight keys. Though nowadays, there are a number of ‘digital piano’ options available – electronic keyboards that do in fact have weighted keys – variations still exist between performance and teaching techniques for both instruments.

Generally, when learning to play piano, students would learn to read music on both the Treble Clef and Bass Clef – right-hand and left-hand lines. Piano music, in comparison to electronic keyboard music, may be more complex in terms of texture and technique and as such, can take slightly longer to master depending on the student.

In contrast, learning electronic keyboard tends to focus more on learning Treble Clef lines only (right-hand) which would be accompanied by simple block chords in the bass/accompaniment section of the instrument (left-hand) – this can be a more expedient and accessible way for students to learn their favourite songs. In addition to this difference, electronic keyboards often come with the facility to play along with backing tracks & rhythmic accompaniment.
